title: - Washoe Lake - Morning
summary: Christian and Marley drove out to Washoe Lake on a cool, cloudy October morning to fly the drone. A hawk landed right in front of them as they arrived, the drone found two groups of wild mustangs near the shore, and the morning ended with a few throws of the ball for Marley.

post.title: Washoe Lake in the morning
post.body:
Marley and I took the truck out to Washoe Lake on the morning of October 21. No bike today: just the ball, the truck and the cameras. I just wanted to fly the drone around a little. It was cloudier than usual and a bit cold, but not too cold, and it was a beautiful morning. The lake was so still it held the whole sky.

It turned out to be a bird day, too. Right as we arrived, around half past seven, a hawk landed in front of us and grabbed something. I'm not sure what. I got a couple of frames of it lifting off low over the dry grass, wings up, with the lake and the hills behind it.

## Tracks in the mud

The water was low. From above, a wide band of grey mud ran between the dry grass and the waterline. It was covered in tracks: tire marks in long curves, and lines of hoofprints running right along the edge of the water.

## Horses on the grass

The hoofprints made sense soon enough. Not long before ten, the drone found two mustangs on their own, out on the dry grass above the lake with the hills behind them. A few hundred feet from those two was another group, a bigger one, grazing under cottonwoods that had already gone yellow. A brown-and-white pinto stood out in front of the rest. I think they're amazing, beautiful animals.

I was far away from all of them, and I didn't stay long enough to count them. I never like disturbing the horses, and I never want to risk spooking them. I always try to ease in, ease away slowly, and stay as far away as I can.

After that I made two more short flights: a slower trip through the trees, and a quick run down the beach.

> It's the kind of morning where the pictures mostly take themselves, and the job is just to keep your distance and not spoil it.

## The same soft light

The browns and golds of the grass, the yellow trees and the blue-grey hills all sat in the same soft light under the cloud. When the flying was done I threw the ball for Marley, and I just enjoyed that. That was basically it.

What I learned: you don't need a plan to make a good morning. Just flying around, I ended up with a hawk, two groups of mustangs and a lake like a mirror.

episode.title: The horses at the water's edge
episode.script:
Narrated by GlazyArray.

It was a cool October morning at Washoe Lake, under more cloud than usual.

Christian had driven out in the truck with Marley. No bike this time. Just the ball, the truck and the cameras. There was no big plan. He just wanted to fly the drone around a little.

The morning started with a bird. Right as they arrived, around half past seven, a hawk landed in front of them and grabbed something. What it was, Christian couldn't say. The hawk wasn't sharing. But he did catch it on camera, lifting off low over the dry grass, wings up, with the lake and the hills behind it.

From up high, the lake was flat as glass, and it held the whole grey and silver sky. The water had pulled back a long way. Between the dry grass and the lake lay a wide band of mud, and the mud was full of stories. Tire tracks swung across it in long, lazy curves. And right along the waterline ran lines of hoofprints.

***

Just before ten, the drone found who had made them.

Two mustangs stood on their own, out on the dry grass, with the lake and the hills behind them. A few hundred feet from those two was another group, a bigger one, grazing under cottonwoods that had already turned yellow. And out in front, a little apart from the rest, stood a brown-and-white pinto. She is the one your eye goes to first in every picture. Or he. I didn't ask.

Christian thinks they're amazing, beautiful animals. So he kept far away from all of them, and he didn't stay to count. He never likes to disturb the horses, or risk spooking them. His way is to ease in, ease away slowly, and keep as far back as he can.

I'll say this for Christian. He let the scene be the scene. The pictures he brought back are calm and wide, with the horses small against the land, and the hills and the water given all the room they want. That's an eye that knows when to step back.

Then he made two more short flights. One was a slow trip through the trees. The other was a quick run down the beach.

***

The whole morning came out in the same few colors. Gold grass. Yellow trees. Blue-grey hills. Silver water.

And when the flying was done, Christian threw the ball for Marley, and he simply enjoyed it. That, more or less, was it.

Some mornings don't need to become anything. This was one of them.

blocks.title: Keep your distance
blocks.text:
On a morning like this one, Christian's rule was a simple one: the pictures mostly take themselves, and the job is just to keep your distance and not spoil it.

It shows in what he brought back. The frames are wide and calm, the horses small against the land, and the hills and the water given all the room they want. Knowing when to step back is its own kind of skill.
